title: SDK integration walkthrough - Acme Financial
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-20
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Redwood SE), Maria Lopez (Acme), Daniel Park (Acme), Sofia Ruiz (Acme)

[00:00] Alex Turner: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, yeah I'm Alex from Redwood, I'll kick us off. Priya and Jordan from the eng team are with me. How's everybody doing?
[00:20] Maria Lopez: Good thanks, busy quarter but excited to see the SDK details. We wanted a practical walkthrough - Python and TypeScript - and to validate auth and env setup for our staging deploys.
[00:45] Priya Shah: Great. Today's plan: quick console overview, then live SDK examples in Python and TS, auth patterns (API key, SSO), env var patterns, and a short Optimize/Console demo for batching and cost controls. We'll leave time for questions and next steps.
[01:15] Daniel Park: We have strict network requirements - VPC peering for dedicated, and we need to know how keys are provisioned. Also latency targets: 150ms p50 for our chat UI, and persistent KV cache for session state.
[02:00] Jordan Kim: Noted. We'll show KV cache options and prefix caching. Quick note, some of the product words in the docs are a little inconsistent - the transcript earlier had "KV cash" typo - but we'll be explicit.
[03:10] Priya Shah: Alright jumping into the Console - opening share screen - here is the Projects page, you can create an org, then a project, then generate API keys. For quickstarts we recommend a project-per-env pattern (dev/stage/prod).
[05:00] Priya Shah: For auth there are two common patterns: short-lived API keys from the Console for service-to-service auth, and SSO/SAML for user access. For production we also support KMS-backed keys and HSM integrations if you need customer-managed keys.
[08:00] Alex Turner: To be specific for SDKs: environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY is the simple path for server-side code. For front-end clients we recommend a proxy pattern or using session tokens with a short TTL - never embed a long-lived key in a bundle.
[12:00] Priya Shah: Now code time. Python quickstart: pip install redwood-sdk (note: package name example), then in quickstart.py: import redwood; client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); response = client.chat.create(...). We have a sample repo at github.com/redwood/quickstarts/python-chat.
[18:00] Maria Lopez: Does the Python SDK support async calls and streaming? We need streaming for the web UI.
[18:20] Priya Shah: Yes, AsyncIO and streaming are supported. Example in the repo: client.chat.stream(...) with an async iterator. Streaming is slightly different across model families so error handling examples are included.
[19:15] Jordan Kim: On TypeScript - npm install @redwoodai/sdk (placeholder), then import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); client.chat.generate(...). For browser use we show a short proxy example in examples/ts/proxy-demo.
[22:30] Daniel Park: For our infra we run services in GCP and some on-prem. How does the SDK handle region routing and fallback?
[23:00] Priya Shah: The SDK respects the endpoint you configure (api.redwood.ai or regional endpoints). For Dedicated we give a private endpoint in your VPC. For hosted customers we have smart routing - you can set policies to prefer low-cost vs low-latency endpoints, and there's automatic fallback to compatible variants if capacity is constrained.
[25:00] Maria Lopez: About batching and cost: how do we control batch size and latency in the SDK?
[25:30] Priya Shah: We expose client-side hints and server-side config. On the client you can set max_batch_tokens, max_batch_wait_ms. The Console Optimize tab will suggest batching profiles based on your latency goals and token distribution. There's also prefix/KV caching which often reduces effective tokens by 30-70% on session-based workloads.
[28:00] Sofia Ruiz: For security/compliance: we need SOC 2 type 2, iso27001 docs, audit logs, and RBAC. Do you support SAML with SCIM for provisioning?
[28:30] Alex Turner: Yes, we support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for enterprise, audit logs at the org and project level, and RBAC with role templates. We'll share the SOC2 reports and a security pack after the call.
[30:00] Daniel Park: Any pitfalls you see when teams integrate the SDK? We've had issues with env var leaks and improper retry logic.
[30:25] Jordan Kim: Common mistakes: embedding long-lived keys in front-end; not handling rate limit 429 responses with exponential backoff; not accounting for chunked streaming errors. We put retry templates in the SDK and best-practice snippets in each quickstart.
[32:00] Priya Shah: Live demo - I'm going to run the Python quickstart against the staging org. (typing) Ok, calling client.chat.create with a 512 token prompt. Response comes back in ~120ms for this short prompt - note this is a small demo model on staging.
[33:30] Maria Lopez: Looks good. For our benchmarks we'll want to run larger sequence lengths and also measure p90/p95 tail latencies.
[34:00] Priya Shah: Absolutely. For POCs we set up a benchmark harness - we can run your prompt sets with pinned model versions and quantization configs, and we'll capture token cost, latency distribution, and memory usage.
[36:00] Alex Turner: On versioning: pin model versions in your code or via project settings in the Console. We support rollout strategies too - canary, A/B, automatic fallback. If you pin and then want to roll, the Console or API can create rollout policies.
[38:00] Sofia Ruiz: For Dedicated/VPC we need details on network diagram, port requirements, and whether private endpoints use mTLS.
[38:20] Jordan Kim: Dedicated nodes can be provisioned with private endpoints and optional mutual TLS. We'll send a network appendix with ports and CIDR requirements.
[40:00] Maria Lopez: What's the onboarding timeline for a POC?
[40:10] Alex Turner: Typically 2-4 weeks: Week 1 account/provisioning + security review, Week 2 benchmark runs, Week 3 analysis and tuning, Week 4 pilot. Dedicated can add provisioning time depending on capacity.
[41:30] Daniel Park: Licensing and pricing - can you recap?
[41:40] Alex Turner: Hosted is usage-based (per-token embedding/generation). Dedicated has reserved capacity contracts, monthly/annual. We also offer Private on-prem licensing. I'll send a tailored pricing sheet.
[42:30] Priya Shah: Quick note on logs & debugging: the SDK emits request IDs you can correlate in the Console tracing. Use the .trace_id in responses for support.
[43:30] Maria Lopez: Great, gives us enough to try the quickstarts. Can you share the repos and security docs?
[43:45] Alex Turner: Yep. We'll send the quickstart repo links, a sample Terraform snippet for env setup, and the SOC2 pack.
[44:00] Sofia Ruiz: We'll review security pack and follow up with any questions.
[44:20] Alex Turner: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with action items and next steps via email.

Notes about transcription: occasional words may be mis-transcribed (e.g., "redwood" vs "red wood"), speaker labels are best-effort.
summary: Redwood AE/SEs walked Acme Financial through SDK quickstarts (Python/TypeScript), auth patterns (API key, SSO/SAML), env setup, Console features for Optimize/batching, and Dedicated/VPC considerations. Agreed next steps: send security pack, sample repos, pricing, and schedule POC benchmark.
